assessment.nobel_worthiness: The optical lattice clock is the clearest case on the list of a measurement technique that changed what can be measured. Trapping neutral atoms at the magic wavelength removes Doppler and recoil shifts while keeping a huge atom number, giving fractional uncertainties near 1e-18. It has opened new work in redefinition of the second, relativistic geodesy, tests of fundamental constants and dark-matter searches.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice concept and made the early strontium demonstrations; Jun Ye brought it to the highest accuracy and stability, with the JILA strontium clocks and many-body clock physics. A two-person prize is clean and well supported. Ye's work builds on the frequency-comb legacy already recognised in 2005, but this is a distinct invention. Other contributors, such as the ion clock groups, are not in the credited list.
assessment.maturity: Mature and independently confirmed by many groups (JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, PTB, NIST, SYRTE and others). Clocks have been compared at the 1e-18 level and are now central to the planned redefinition of the second, so recognition is timely.
uncertainties: Whether the committee sees the lattice clock as sufficiently separate from earlier frequency-metrology prizes.
Credit for the original magic-wavelength idea versus the later accuracy record: Katori's priority is clear in the supplied text, but other early lattice proposals are not described.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Matter-wave interferometry with laser-manipulated atoms provides inertial and gravitational sensors of exceptional sensitivity. Its uses include measurements of g and G, the fine-structure constant, gravity gradiometry and equivalence-principle tests. It is a real new way of observing nature.
assessment.attribution: Bordé's atom-interferometer theory and Ramsey-Bordé fringes, Pritchard's early atom-optics and interferometry experiments (gratings and light-pulse beam splitters) and Kasevich/Chu's light-pulse gravimeter and gradiometer all matter. The supplied trio is workable, but Steven Chu, Chu's group and Chu's earlier prize in 1997 complicate a clean story. The names as credited exclude Chu and Chu's group, which I cannot resolve from this packet.
assessment.maturity: Mature and widely reproduced, with commercial gravimeters and large-scale projects. Applications such as navigation and geodesy are real but still developing, and fundamental-physics results remain precision tests rather than discoveries.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 1997 laser-cooling prize and the contribution of Steven Chu, who is not in the credited names.
Priority between the Bordé/Pritchard line (beam splitters, interferometry) and the light-pulse gravimeter line (Kasevich).

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Squeezed light turned a theoretical noise limit into a practical sensitivity gain. Caves showed that squeezed vacuum can beat the shot-noise limit in interferometers, Kimble's group made the early experimental demonstrations, and GEO600 and LIGO now operate with squeezed light as a routine upgrade. This is a direct case of a quantum optics technique enabling a measurement that had a Nobel-level impact (gravitational waves).
assessment.attribution: Caves is the decisive theorist for the interferometer proposal. Kimble led an early experimental demonstration of squeezing, and Schnabel led the implementation in GEO600 and later detectors. Important contributors are missing from the credited list, notably Slusher and the Walls and Yurke theory groups, and the LIGO/GEO implementers; the proposed three are defensible but not complete.
assessment.maturity: Mature in the sense that it is deployed in operating detectors and provides measurable gains, with independent confirmation by GEO600, LIGO and Virgo. Frequency-dependent squeezing is still being refined.
uncertainties: Attribution is spread over many groups, and the supplied trio omits experimental pioneers.
Whether the field is better recognised through gravitational-wave detection prizes already awarded.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The Cirac-Zoller proposal for quantum gates with trapped ions and the experimental realisation of ion-based quantum logic, entanglement and algorithms made the first physically credible quantum computer architecture. Ion-trap processors remain among the leading platforms for fidelity and coherence.
assessment.attribution: Cirac and Zoller made the 1995 proposal; Blatt's group demonstrated the Cirac-Zoller gate and many key experiments, including teleportation and multi-qubit entanglement. The omission of Wineland (who shared the 2012 prize) and of other ion groups such as Monroe and Wineland's NIST group is a concern. A prize for Cirac, Zoller and Blatt is plausible but must be argued against the 2012 prize.
assessment.maturity: Mature: gate fidelities above 99.9% are now reproduced in many groups, and commercial machines exist. Timeliness is good given the recent 2025 prize for superconducting-circuit macroscopic quantum effects.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2012 Wineland and Haroche prize and the missing Monroe and Wineland credit.
Whether the committee prefers the theory or experiment framing.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical detection and coherent control of single NV centre spins in diamond made a room-temperature solid-state qubit and a quantum sensor with nanoscale resolution. It has opened magnetometry, thermometry, nanoscale NMR and biological sensing, and I find the impact beyond physics persuasive.
assessment.attribution: Wrachtrup (first single-NV optical detection, 1997) and Jelezko (coherent control and the nuclear-spin register) are the experimental core. Lukin contributed major theory-experiment work on NV sensing and on quantum registers, but he also appears in other candidates, and other NV pioneers such as Awschalom, Hanson and Hollenberg are not credited.
assessment.maturity: Mature as a method, with extensive independent replication. Sensor applications are still moving from demonstration to routine instruments, so the long-term impact is not fully visible.
uncertainties: Comparative claims of Wrachtrup/Jelezko against Awschalom, Hanson and others who are not in the credited names.
Lukin appears in several candidates, so a prize configuration would need a decision about which of his contributions to recognise.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The experimental discovery of the Higgs boson by ATLAS and CMS confirmed the final missing part of the Standard Model and was an extraordinary instrumentation and measurement achievement. The detector design, trigger and analysis were decisive.
assessment.attribution: The 2013 prize went to the theorists (Englert and Higgs), so a second prize would recognise the experiment. The credited names are the founding spokespersons and conveners. Choosing three from thousands of collaborators is inherently arbitrary, and the Nobel statutes limit this. I propose the early proposers and leaders of the two collaborations (Della Negra, Jenni, Virdee), but Gianotti's role as spokesperson at the announcement is a reasonable alternative.
assessment.maturity: Fully mature and independently confirmed by two experiments and by later coupling measurements. Recognition is arguably overdue, but the attribution problem is the obstacle rather than the science.
uncertainties: How to credit a collaboration of thousands within the three-person limit.
Whether the experiment is now seen as already honoured by the 2013 prize.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Circuit QED made strong coupling of superconducting qubits to microwave photons routine, giving dispersive readout, gates and the main architecture for superconducting quantum processors. Its measurement-and-control toolbox is now widely used.
assessment.attribution: Blais provided the theory, Wallraff and Schoelkopf the 2004 experimental demonstration with the Yale group. The credited trio is coherent and fits well. The recent 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits makes the field's recognition timing delicate.
assessment.maturity: Mature and replicated by dozens of groups; the technology is under heavy industrial development. Timeliness is reasonable but the 2025 prize could be seen as already covering this area.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2025 prize for superconducting circuit quantum effects.
Whether the main impact is the physics concept or the engineering platform.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Horizon-scale imaging of M87* and Sgr A* is a landmark of observational technique: a global VLBI array at 1.3 mm with extreme calibration and imaging methods. It gives direct tests of strong-gravity predictions.
assessment.attribution: Falcke proposed the shadow-imaging idea, Doeleman led the EHT technical development, and Zensus built the European VLBI side; the EHT collaboration has hundreds of members, so a three-person selection leaves credit unresolved.
assessment.maturity: Results from 2019 and 2022 are well established but the interpretation (spin, ring size, jet) is still developing, and independent confirmation beyond EHT itself is limited. It may be early compared with the others.
uncertainties: Independence of confirmation: only one collaboration has produced the images.
Allocation of credit within a large collaboration.
